o: Maximize (subarray sum) × (subarray gcd) over subarrays of length ≥ k. Brute force is O(n²) gcd extensions. The crucial structural fact: as the left endpoint of subarrays ending at index i moves left, the gcd takes at most O(log(max)) distinct values, each over a contiguous range of left endpoints. For each such gcd segment [L..i] with gcd g, the best choice is the longest allowed suffix (start = max(L, i−k+1)), since a larger sum with the same gcd is always better. Example 1: [4,4,4] gives g=4, sum=12 → 48.
k: GCDs of subarrays ending at i take O(log V) distinct values over contiguous left ranges.
For fixed gcd, longer subarray ⇒ larger product, so take the longest suffix within the segment subject to length ≥ k.
Prefix sums give O(1) range sums.

a.i: For each right endpoint, extend leftward maintaining gcd and running sum; update the answer when length ≥ k. Simple, O(n² log V) — fine for small n, instructive baseline.
s: For each i, walk j from i down to 0 updating g = gcd(g, nums[j]) and s += nums[j]

a.i: Keep a list of (gcd, leftmostIndex) segments for subarrays ending at the current index; each step re-gcds with the new element and merges equal neighbors (list stays O(log V)). For each segment, evaluate the longest valid suffix via prefix sums.
s: For each i, rebuild the segment list with gcd(g, nums[i]), appending [nums[i], i] if the last gcd differs
For each segment, candidate = g · (P[i+1] − P[max(L, i−k+1)])
a.t: O(n log V · log n) — the segment list has O(log V) entries per step, each gcd costs log V

w: Lead with the brute force to show understanding, then upgrade to the segment trick — it's the classic 'gcd of all subarrays ending here' technique. Products reach 10⁵ × 10⁶ × 10⁶-scale sums, so 64-bit (or BigInt in JS) is mandatory. Pitfall: evaluating only the full segment instead of the longest valid suffix misses cases where k cuts into the segment.
